# Part V — Index

## 18. Segments, manifests and the per-file fact store

The index is a set of immutable, checksummed segments (`docs/design/contracts/SEGMENTS-v1.md`,
`crates/dctx-map-segment`, `crates/dctx-adapter-store`) under the cache root. No SQLite,
no daemon.

```text
<cache root>/v2/<root-id>/
  facts/<FactKey-prefix>/<FactKey>.seg   per-file fact segments; a changed file reparses one segment
  views/<generation>/view.seg            nodes, forward and reverse adjacency, postings, dictionary
  views/<generation>/manifest.man        sorted path → (stamp, ObjectKey, FactKey)
  current.ptr                            atomic pointer to the published generation
  answers/<session>.ledger               delta and dedup ledger (§12.3–12.4)
```

- Identical files parse once across roots (shared `FactKey`).
- Publication uses a writer lock, staging, pointer swap, leases and a previous pointer
  for recovery (landed protocol; formal model in `docs/formal/dctx-cache`).
- Cache lifecycle: time-based expiry, a size cap and a bounded automatic cleaner
  (landed defaults: 7 days idle overlays, 30 days unpinned roots, 2 GiB hard cap).
- Readers validate section checksums lazily on first touch; the envelope checksum is
  mandatory at publication.
- Generations are content-addressed: an unchanged snapshot digest publishes no new
  bytes (today three byte-identical 158 MB generations of one root were stored).
  Superseded, unpinned generations of the same root are reclaimable at the next
  invocation; the unlink grace period applies to orphaned objects, not to superseded
  generations (today a one-day grace let a root grow from 158 MB to 946 MB while
  `cache gc --dry-run` reclaimed 0 bytes, TC-F02).

## 19. Freshness check and incremental rebuild

**Status: target, not implemented.** The shipped engine has no stamp-only pass, overlay or
per-file rebuild: each process re-walks and re-hashes, and any change rebuilds fully (R3, §3).

1. **Stamp pass.** Walk the inventory (names, sizes, mtimes; excluded directories are
   never entered) and compare with the manifest's sorted path table.
2. **Digest pass** only for entries whose stamp differs, plus the query's dependency
   scope under `strict_live`. `read` always verifies its own bytes.
3. **Rebuild.** Changed files reparse one fact segment each; their nodes and edges are
   masked by an overlay; references that named symbols they declare (or now declare) are
   re-resolved through the reverse unresolved-name index; the result publishes as an
   overlay generation. Overlays compact into the base past a threshold. An unchanged
   snapshot digest reuses the published generation without writing.

| Gate | Target | Measured today (§31.0) |
|---|---|---|
| `dctx map status` | ≤50 ms p95 | no verb |
| Warm `find` / `neighbors` / `read`, small and medium corpora | ≤30 ms engine p95, ≤80 ms process | 0.03–0.26 s process (comparison 0.69–1.40 s) |
| Warm `find` / `neighbors` / `read`, largest corpus (core, 3,190 files) | ≤0.8 s process, ≤150 MiB | 1.45 s, 370 MiB (comparison `callers` 0.83 s) |
| First query after a one-line edit | ≤2× warm | ≈ cold (core 7.48 s against 1.45 s warm; django 2.70 s against 0.82 s) |
| Cache per root after 10 edits | ≤1.5× one generation | 6× (158 MB → 946 MB after about five edits) |
| Single-file reindex | ≤50 ms | n/a |
| Correctness | Answers byte-identical to a cold rebuild | — |

## 20. Cold build

Parallel parsing with a bounded parser thread pool (`std::thread::scope`, ≤ available
parallelism); each thread owns its fact segments; a single sealer merges sorted outputs
and hashes incrementally without materializing a joined payload. Policy caps facts per
file (`extraction.max_facts_per_file`, default 10,000); excess configuration and JSON
leaves collapse into one `partial` module node.

**Gate:** cold build ≤5 s and peak RSS ≤150 MiB on the pinned corpus; persistent bytes
≤40 MiB. Measured today (§31.0): core (3,190 files) 6.05 s / 567 MiB; django (7,071
files) 2.48 s / 92 MiB; flask (235 files) 0.09 s / 8 MiB. Cold indexing is 2.8 to 69
times faster than the comparison tool on all seven corpora with 1.6 to 27 times less
peak memory, and MUST stay at or below half of its time per corpus.

## 21. Ranking

Lexical scoring over identifiers split on case and separators, path segments and the
first doc line; exact-name boost; kind and path filters; confidence-aware boosts for
graph neighbors of the focus set. Integer scores; ties broken by id; the scoring
revision is versioned and part of the view digest.

# Part VI — Extension

## 22. Core, surface or plugin: the decision procedure

```text
Does it read or write anything other than authorized source bytes, the dctx cache root
or a caller-supplied sink?
  no  → core: engine or adapter (first-party crate, std-only target)
  yes → does it only transport answers the core already produced, deciding nothing about content?
          yes → surface adapter (compiled in behind a feature: CLI, MCP, hook-file generator)
          no  → plugin (out of process, brokered, consented, receipted)
Does it need a socket, a subprocess or a foreign runtime (language server, compiler, model)?
  yes → plugin; never core; never a default-on effect
Does it change selection, identity, freshness, ranking or budgets?
  yes → refused as a plugin capability
```

| Component | Placement |
|---|---|
| Ids, spans, budgets, selection, digest, DTS compiler, segment codec, resolver, binder | Pure core |
| 13 lexer crates covering 15 language variants (Rust, JS, TS, TSX, Markdown, Python, Go, Java, C/C++, JSON/TOML/YAML, C#, Kotlin, Ruby, PHP, Swift); `syn` adapter | Core engine |
| Filesystem source, cache, segment store | Adapters |
| CLI, MCP server, agent-hook generator, statusline | Surfaces |
| Git (`.gitignore` protection, staging, `vcs.changes`) | First-party plugin (bundled) |
| Language-server / SCIP edges | First-party plugin, edge overlay |
| CI and pull-request comments | Plugin with the v2 network capability |
| Telemetry | Does not exist |
| Model calls | Never in dctx; summaries only by fingerprint-bound import |

## 23. Plugin protocol and its v1.x extensions

The plugin host is landed: a grant lattice with explicit denies, policy epochs with
re-checks at admission and commit, receipts and a ledger, liveness by progress (not
timers), signed distribution with pinned keys and revocation, Linux confinement, and
TLA+ models with mutation witnesses (`docs/design/PLUGINS.md`, `docs/formal/dctx-plugins`).
Properties PP1–PP10 hold for every extension below.

### 23.1 New capabilities and hooks (target, negotiated minor versions)

| Addition | Kind | Contract |
|---|---|---|
| `vcs.changes {scope: staged \| worktree \| range}` | Broker request (git plugin) | Bounded `{path, added, removed}` hunks; paths filtered by current selection |
| `facts.overlay {generation, segment}` | Broker request (overlay plugins) | Uploads an edge-only overlay segment with provenance; the host checks every endpoint exists and no row touches an excluded path; never merged into fact segments |
| `after-query` | Advisory hook | Verb, record ids, bytes and budget use — never record contents |
| `on-source-changed` | Advisory hook | Fired when a generation publishes; payload is the changed path list after selection |
| `network.post {origin, max_bytes}` | Capability (protocol v2) | Separate consent, organization egress allowlist, receipts with response digest; off in every default |

### 23.2 The compiler-grade overlay (`dctx/lsp`, `dctx/scip`)

Spawns a configured language server under confinement (no project writes, no network),
asks for definitions and references of the view's `name`-confidence and unresolved
references in bounded batches, and uploads an edge overlay labeled
`exact (lsp:<server>@<version>)`. `--no-overlay` disables it per request. SCIP import is
the batch variant for CI. Neither is a default; neither changes `FactKey`.

## 24. Surfaces

### 24.1 CLI

One binary: `dctx` (pack, map, template, cache, plugin, policy, agent, learn, check,
blast, serve). Interactive TUI when run without arguments.

### 24.2 Library facade

`crates/dctx` is the stable API for every surface (`docs/design/contracts/API-PORTS-v1.md`).
Bindings for Python, Node and a C ABI wrap the facade; none re-implements an engine.

### 24.3 MCP server

`dctx mcp [PATH]` (also `dctx serve --mcp`) speaks JSON-RPC over stdio, one message
per line. The default tools are `map`, `find`, `neighbors`, `explain`, `read`, `hubs`,
`grep`, `skeleton`, `path` and `export`; each runs the corresponding `dctx map` verb.
`--profile lean` exposes only `find` and `read`; `--profile three` exposes only
`map`, `find` and `read`; `--tools NAME,...` selects a custom subset. Selected tools
have shorter descriptions and retain complete input schemas.
Unselected tools cannot be called. The default surface is unchanged.

See the [MCP guide](guides/MCP.md) for configuration, validation and startup response
sizes. Measure whole agent sessions against grep plus reading files, including
instructions, tool definitions and extra calls. Wire bytes and bytes/4 estimates
alone do not establish total session token savings. Tool results use the CLI's code
path and MUST NOT contain instructions to the agent, banners or requests to report
savings.

### 24.4 Agent hooks (target)

`dctx agent install <host> [--project]` renders, from the effective policy, the host's
own configuration fragment: a statusline that runs `dctx map status`, a session-start
injection of tiers T0–T2 (≤1,000 tokens, placed after the host's stable prompt prefix),
and the guidance "use `dctx map find` / `read` before grep and cat". Installation is a
user-consented file write with a receipt, idempotent (marker line) and reversible
(`dctx agent uninstall`). Organization policy can allow, require or forbid hosts. No
daemon, no watcher.

### 24.5 Desktop

The desktop app is **free, forever**. It is a surface over the same facade: snapshots,
settings, recent projects, plugin management. It has no engine or cache behaviour of
its own and is never part of the CLI or library dependency closure.

## 25. Blast radius (target)

`dctx blast` traverses reverse adjacency (callers, implementors, tests, documents) from a
set of changed spans, bounded like `neighbors`. The graph side is core. The change side
has two sources, neither of which puts a VCS in the core:

1. **Snapshot diff (default).** `dctx blast --from <snapshot>` compares the current
   source snapshot with a retained one. Works in any directory.
2. **VCS supply.** The git plugin's `vcs.changes` returns hunks for `--staged`,
   `--branch <name>` and similar; the core maps hunks to node spans.

Formats: text records, JSON, and `--format pr-comment` (Markdown). Posting the comment
is a network plugin. **Gate:** ≤100 ms warm for a 10-hunk change on the pinned corpus.

## 26. Learnings (target)

Teams lose decisions and guardrails to chat logs. dctx keeps them as plain files next to
the code, without becoming a memory product.

| Aspect | Rule |
|---|---|
| Location | `.dctx/learnings/<kind>/<slug>.md`; kinds `decisions`, `guardrails`, `preferences`, `skills`; policy may narrow kinds and size |
| Format | Markdown; first heading is the title; a fenced `dctx` block with `applies:` ids, `since:` snapshot, `status: active \| retired`, optional `enforce: true` |
| Indexing | Ordinary `d:` doc nodes with `documents` edges to the ids they name; `find --kind learning`; boost when `applies` meets the focus set |
| Authoring | `dctx learn add <kind> "<title>" [--applies <id>…]`. The core writes only into `.dctx/learnings/` and only on an explicit user action |
| Sharing | It is content: shared through version control like any file; the git plugin may stage it when granted |
| `dctx check` | For each changed node (§25), lists guardrails whose `applies` covers it or its neighbors at depth 1. Advisory; exit non-zero only with `--strict` and an enforced active guardrail |
| Freshness | A learning that applies to a `gone` id is reported `orphaned`; nothing is deleted automatically |
| Model-written text | Only via `dctx learn import` with body-fingerprint binding; labeled `src=import:<tag>`; served only while fingerprints match |

# Part VII — Assurance

## 27. Dependencies and build profiles

All first-party code and documentation are Apache-2.0, copyright Eris Margeta,
including the desktop app and planned GPUI rebuild. This section records build
engineering goals, not an edition, license tier or certification of suitability.
The current dependency inventories are [THIRD_PARTY.md](../THIRD_PARTY.md) and
[THIRD_PARTY_NPM.md](../THIRD_PARTY_NPM.md); inspect manifests and features for an
exact build's closure. Earlier 0.25.0 dependency counts are historical measurements.

### 27.1 The rules

- **Core crates are std-only.** `dctx-hash`, `dctx-core`, `dctx-ports`, `dctx-map-model`
  (without `wire-json`), `dctx-map-segment`, `dctx-template`, `dctx-pack`,
  `dctx-map-resolve`, `dctx-map-bind`, `dctx-plugin-protocol`, the hand-written lexers,
  `dctx-adapter-fs`, `dctx-adapter-store`, `dctx-adapter-cache` and `dctx-map-scan`
  have zero third-party normal dependencies and forbid `unsafe`; CI checks
  `cargo tree -e normal` per crate.
- **Every third-party crate in a default build is listed** in `docs/DEPENDENCIES.md`
  with version, licence, `unsafe` count, reason and the plan for it. CI fails if the
  closure grows beyond the list.
- **Ed25519 stays for security and trust.** `ed25519-dalek` (exact pin, `std` feature
  only, verify-only) is a vetted, widely audited security crate and the **single
  disclosed exception** to the zero-third-party rule, behind feature `trust`. It
  verifies the signatures on plugins and organization policy bundles. A build without
  `trust` has no third-party crate and cannot verify signatures; it refuses unsigned
  bundles rather than trusting them. Audited cryptography is not replaced by something
  less proven; the search for the best long-term solution continues, and any successor
  must clear the same bar (RFC 8032 and Wycheproof vectors, differential fuzzing,
  independent review).

### 27.2 Planned removals

| Remove | First-party replacement | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| `syn` from the `strict` feature | Today `strict` implies `syntax-rust`; a minimal feature set MUST NOT (structural Rust extractor with `precision.parser = dctx-structural/1`) | Build proves the closure |
| `serde`, `serde_json`, `thiserror`, production `sha2` | The facade's hand-written canonical JSON; std `Error`; `dctx-hash` | Goldens byte-identical |
| `rusqlite` and bundled SQLite | The immutable segment index (§18) | Segment index beats the SQLite baseline on two of latency, disk and refresh with no quality loss |
| `syn` stack from the default build | First-party Rust structural extractor + binder (§7.1) | Held-out precision ≥ `syn` − 1 point; zero wrong `exact` edges |
| Linux confinement crates | Kept as a disclosed, target-specific adapter dependency outside the minimal closure (plugins unavailable in that build), or a reviewed first-party syscall boundary in `dctx-plugin-platform` | Confinement property tests; written `unsafe` review |

The desktop app is a separate surface over the facade and is never part of the CLI or
library closure.

### 27.3 Maintenance

dctx is Apache-2.0 open source, including the desktop app, with no license fee. Organizations that depend on dctx can sign a maintenance agreement for security response targets, long-term support and priority work; see [MAINTENANCE.md](../MAINTENANCE.md). Build-closure targets are engineering goals.

| Suite | What it proves |

| Verb goldens (`docs/design/contracts/GOLDEN-REQUESTS-v1.json`) | Byte-identical pages across OS, thread count and surface |

TLA+ models with mutation witnesses cover the cache lifecycle (`docs/formal/dctx-cache`)

base change).

## 30. Versioning and compatibility

Independent version axes: library API, wire format (text page, JSON v2), DTS source,
plan IR, identity, segments, cache layout, plugin protocol, policy bundle. Each axis
has a major/minor rule; readers refuse unknown required sections; a version
declaration selects behaviour — it is never inferred from an unknown field.

empty or thin (no edges, id-only text pages, no bounded overview, no text search, no
multi-word search). The roadmap below closes those holes first, with code that already
exists, before the architectural work.

### 31.1 Phases

All gates are measured by rerunning the benchmark scripts on the same pinned corpora and

P0 and P1 turn a 69-of-140 tool into a ≥ 115-of-140 tool with changes measured in days,
using lexers and a resolver that already exist. P2 is the one architectural piece, and
it is also where dctx loses to the comparison tool on the largest corpus. P3 is the

## 32. Non-goals

| Not doing | Why |
|---|---|
| Embeddings or a vector index in the core | Non-deterministic, model-dependent, hides provenance (R2, R8) |
| Calling a model from the engine | Breaks determinism; spends the tokens the tool exists to save |
| A daemon or file watcher | One binary, no runtime; a per-invocation stamp check meets 50 ms |
| VCS in the core | Privacy and dependency reasons; everything needed is a plugin or dctx's own snapshot diff |
| A second configuration language | Two policy engines diverge; DTS already compiles to a sealed IR |
| Telemetry, even opt-out | Trust is the product |
| A hosted index or SaaS | Changes the threat model |
| Parser injection or selection override by plugins | Would make identity and privacy unverifiable |
| Chasing language counts | 13 lexers covering 15 language variants, each with precision labels, beat 23 with silent errors (the comparison tool indexed 8 of 13 planted extra-language files; dctx indexed none and said so); each new language needs a held-out corpus |
| mmap or FST before measurement | Requires a ≥20 % measured gain first |
| In-band agent instructions in answers | Tool output is data; a banner costs tokens on every call and changes with the covered files |

# What dctx is

dctx turns any folder into the smallest correct context for a task, offline, with byte-stable output that prompt caches can reuse.

“Smallest correct context” describes the goal, not a proof that task selection
is complete or minimal. The shipped engine selects lexical symbols and document
sections, verifies source reads and bounds answers. A 200 GB folder needs a
relevant sub-root and ignore rules; output budgets do not bound scanning.
Byte stability enables reuse, while provider cache rules determine actual hits.
dctx has no embeddings, network, telemetry or agent loop in its pack/map/MCP
workflows. It does not call a model or execute the task for you.

> dctx is an advanced tool with several ways to use it. Used well, it cuts the context an agent needs to a fraction. Used without a plan, it can add calls and tokens instead of removing them. If you are new, follow the safe path: one project, the system binary, the lean MCP profile. Measure before you change anything.

## Choose your path

Choose one of these four paths. Each starts with a shipped workflow; the planned
scope and distribution features are labeled explicitly.

1. [One giant folder](#one-giant-folder)
2. [Many small projects](#many-small-projects)
3. [Agent builder embedding a library](#agent-builder-embedding-a-library)
4. [Team / enterprise admin](#team--enterprise-admin)

### One giant folder

One giant folder (e.g. 200 GB): system binary; per-root ignore policy; name a sub-root/--place in tasks. Pitfall: pointing agents at the whole root.

Install the [system binary](#safe-path-in-ten-minutes), choose a relevant package,
and put exclusions in that root's `.dctxignore` before the first query:

```sh
dctx map find Config --place packages/service-a --budget 500 --limit 5
```

Expect bounded symbol IDs and line ranges, not a complete answer about the whole
parent tree. Use an ID with `map read`. There is no general receipt yet;
`--json` exposes freshness, precision and pagination. Each invocation checks
source stamps; no daemon or file watcher is used. Catalog-first sharding and a
unified policy file are planned. Read the
[huge-tree limits and ignore example](MODALITIES.md#huge-trees-scope-before-indexing)
before warming an index; `--in` only filters after indexing.

### Many small projects

Many small projects: system binary; lean MCP once in the agent config; nothing per project. Pitfall: stale caches of deleted projects -> cache gc/purge.

Install one binary and configure the [lean MCP profile](guides/MCP.md) in your
agent. The config can live at user scope; launch the server with the intended
project root for each session. No project dependency is required. Start with a
`find` call followed by `read` using its exact ID. Expect source plus freshness
and precision in JSON, not a general receipt or session delta.

```sh
dctx cache status --json
dctx cache gc --dry-run
dctx cache purge --root /absolute/deleted-project --dry-run
```

Inspect the dry run before applying cleanup; `purge` requires `--yes`.
See [cache controls](guides/MAP-MODE.md#index-cache-and-privacy). Indexes live in an
engine `major.minor` subdirectory (for example `1.3`) of the cache parent, which is
`DCTX_CACHE_DIR` or the platform default `v2` cache root; patch releases share it, and
data from other engine versions is ignored.

### Agent builder embedding a library

Agent builder embedding a library: project library with its own pinned binary (Python, Node or Go wrapper over `dctx rpc`; registry publication pending); never parse or slice pack text. Pitfall: re-implementing engine logic.

The [Python](../packages/python/README.md), [Node](../packaging/npm/dctx/README.md)
and [Go](../packages/go/README.md) wrappers over `dctx rpc` are built and tested in
CI, but not yet published to PyPI, npm or a Go module proxy; install them from CI
artifacts or a checkout as their READMEs describe. Alternatively, pin the
[Rust facade](MODALITIES.md#rust-library-embed-the-facade) from tagged Git,
or invoke the installed CLI as a subprocess. The first runnable Rust example is
in the [library doctest](../examples/library/README.md). For subprocess use:

```sh
dctx map find Config --json --budget 500 --limit 5
```

Expect JSON records with IDs and precision/freshness metadata; pass a returned
ID to `map read --json` for `source_utf8`. Keep engine selection and rendering in
the engine. Pass opaque continuation cursors back unchanged rather than slicing
pack text. [Named context](CONTEXT.md) adds stable chunk IDs and opt-in delivery
sessions: use `dctx context TARGET --session ID --dedupe`, or the existing MCP
`read` tool with `context: true`. Delivery history lasts for the CLI invocation
or MCP/RPC connection; general receipts remain planned. A Rust facade `Session`
is an in-process API object. See the [scope contract](#two-scopes-one-binary).

### Team / enterprise admin

Team / enterprise admin: system binary via package manager, signature + SBOM verification, one pinned version fleet-wide. Pitfall: mixing project and system versions without checking (`dctx doctor`).

This is the rollout target. Today, pin a release archive and check its matching
`SHA256SUMS` entry; package-manager distribution, signed CLI binaries and a
release SBOM verification workflow are planned. Deploy the verified archive and
root ignore rules through your existing fleet tooling. Record the resolved
binary path and start with:

```sh
dctx --version --verbose
```

Expect version and feature/precision limits. `dctx doctor` lists the dctx
binaries visible from a directory with their scopes and SHA-256 checksums;
signature-status output is planned. Check paths and versions explicitly during onboarding;
use [release procedure](../RELEASING.md), [testing](TESTING.md) and
[security reporting](../SECURITY.md) for the current controls. Signed
organization policy bundles and audit journals are planned.

## Safe path in ten minutes

### 1. Install the system binary

Download the archive for your OS and architecture and `SHA256SUMS` from
[GitHub Releases](https://github.com/Eris-Margeta/dctx/releases/tag/v1.3.0).
Compare the archive's SHA-256 with its matching entry before extracting it.
On Linux use `sha256sum ARCHIVE`, on macOS `shasum -a 256 ARCHIVE`, or on Windows
PowerShell `Get-FileHash ARCHIVE -Algorithm SHA256`, replacing `ARCHIVE` with the
downloaded filename. This checks integrity against the release checksums;
signed binary verification is planned.

Extract the archive and put `dctx` (`dctx.exe` on Windows) on your user `PATH`.
Archives cover Linux x64/ARM64, macOS x64/ARM64 and Windows x64.

```sh
dctx --version
```

Use the system binary for interactive agents. The project wrappers (Python, Node,
Go) are built and tested in CI, with registry publication pending; no project
dependency is needed for this path.

### 2. Choose one project and inspect one answer

Use a small project or a relevant sub-root. Check `.gitignore` and `.dctxignore`
before scanning; leave `DCTX_INDEX_IGNORED` unset. From that directory:

```sh
dctx map find Config --json --budget 500 --limit 5
```

Replace `Config` with a symbol or heading in your project. Read a returned ID
with `dctx map read 'ID' --json`. The JSON includes verified source bytes as
`source_utf8` and reports precision, freshness and pagination. Keep the same
root between calls, because root-relative IDs change when the root changes.

### 3. Configure the lean MCP profile

In a client accepting `mcpServers`, replace both absolute paths:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "dctx": {
      "command": "/absolute/path/to/dctx",
      "args": ["mcp", "--profile", "lean", "/absolute/path/to/project"]
    }
  }
}
```

Restart the client and confirm that `find` and `read` are available. The lean
profile has **two tools**, not the planned `context/read/find` profile. For a
controlled comparison, turn off overlapping host file tools where the client
allows it; keep instructions and task scope consistent. Use the
[MCP guide](guides/MCP.md) for profile selection and measured startup overhead,
and [client-specific configs](MODALITIES.md#client-configuration) for other formats.

### 4. Measure before changing anything

Run the same small task with grep plus narrow file reads and with lean MCP.
Record task correctness, number of tool calls, startup instructions and schemas,
all model input/output tokens, provider cache hits, latency and billed cost when
available. Include the history carried into each model turn. Smaller tool
answers alone do not establish whole-session savings.

General receipts are planned. Today, retain JSON metadata and the agent's usage
report. For task packs, the shipped footer is a useful output accounting line:

```sh
dctx pack . --for 'Config' --budget 800
```

It reports `body_tokens`, `budget` and `dropped`, using estimated tokens rather
than a provider tokenizer. It is not a whole-session receipt. Save outputs
outside the selected tree, and compare repeated runs with identical inputs.
See [measurement evidence](BENCHMARK-20261030.md) and
[CI/cache guidance](MODALITIES.md#ci--prompt-cache-prefix-stability).

## Responsibilities

This table uses the scope contract's wording, with unshipped provisions marked
`(planned)`. Prebuilt archives with `SHA256SUMS` exist today; signed CLI binary
releases do not. ACP setup is planned; the MCP lean profile and its startup
measurement exist.

| Level | dctx provides | You are responsible for |
|---|---|---|
| System binary | Release archives with cosign signatures, SBOM and provenance, cache caps, `dctx doctor`, journals (planned), receipts (planned) | Choosing roots, policy file, keeping one version on PATH |
| Project library | Pinned vendored binary and protocol client (Python, Node, Go wrappers; registry publication pending), same bytes as CLI (checked in CI) | Pinning the version, exclusions in the project policy, not re-implementing engine logic |
| MCP and ACP agent setup | Lean profile, tested client configs, measured start-up cost | Turning off the host's own file tools, picking a profile, session ids, reading receipts |
| CI and cache | Byte-stable pack, prefix tiers (planned), deterministic exit codes | Pinning the binary, caching the index between runs, treating pack drift as a signal not noise |

For current CLI exclusions, use `.gitignore` and `.dctxignore`; the unified policy
file is planned. Agent session ids and general receipts in the responsibility
column describe planned integrations. The Rust facade exists today with explicit
host-supplied selection and storage policy; the project-library row describes
the Python, Node and Go wrappers, which are not yet on a public registry. Existing pack prefix stability is distinct
from the planned layered prefix tiers.

## Two scopes, one binary

The following is the distribution contract for the project-library wrappers
(registry publication pending) and signed releases:

> The system `dctx` on PATH belongs to you and your agents. A binary installed by a project library lives inside that project (virtualenv, node_modules), pinned and managed by that package manager. Same signed engine, different owner. Interactive agents and MCP call the system binary; application code and CI call the project binary; a library never silently falls back to PATH.

Today, install the system binary from release archives. The Python, Node and Go
wrappers already follow the no-fallback contract: they resolve an explicit path,
`DCTX_BIN`, their own platform package (Python, Node) or a versioned user cache,
and never search `PATH`. Until they are published, install them from CI
artifacts or a checkout, or invoke an explicitly pinned CLI path. The Rust facade
is an in-process library, not a vendored executable.

The CLI cache lives in `<cache-parent>/<engine-major.minor>/` under the
platform-specific `dctx/v2` parent (or `DCTX_CACHE_DIR`), so engines 1.2 and 1.3
keep separate indexes while patch releases of one family share theirs (see
[scopes](SCOPES.md)). A version/path line in every pack is planned. Today
`dctx rpc` reports the engine version in `hello`, and `dctx doctor` lists the dctx
binaries visible from a directory. Check the executable path and version
explicitly, and use separate absolute `DCTX_CACHE_DIR` locations when two
installations of the same engine family must not share an index. Both future scopes should read the project's exclusions; today the
CLI loads ignore files while a Rust host supplies its own selection rules.

Continue with the [documentation index](README.md), [modalities](MODALITIES.md)
or [engine specification](SPEC.md).

# Why dctx exists

What problem dctx solves, the rules it follows, and why "byte-identical output" matters even if you never think about bytes.

## The problem

An AI coding assistant only knows what is in its **context window**: the text sent to the model with your request. It cannot see the rest of your project.

Most projects are too large to send whole, so tools pick pieces. Often they pick badly: whole files when one function would do, text that looks similar but is the wrong code, code as it was before your last edit, or half a function.

Each of these costs you. Models read text as **tokens** (small chunks of text, roughly a short word or part of one), and providers bill per token. The model reads every token before it answers, so more tokens also means more waiting. And answers get worse as irrelevant text piles up. The [README](../README.md#the-core-belief-prompt-processing-efficiency) sums it up: every token in front of a model is paid for three times, to read it, again when a cache is missed, and again in attention.

## What dctx does

dctx is a command-line tool that reads your project on your machine and answers precise questions about it: where a function is defined, what calls it, what its exact source is. Each answer fits a size budget and is built from whole pieces of syntax; a piece that is too long is marked as cut, with a way to get the rest. The same question about the same code gives the same bytes every time. An assistant can run the commands itself or call them through the built-in MCP server (`dctx mcp`; MCP is a standard way for AI tools to call other tools). dctx can also pack a whole project into one structured block for a chat.

### Start with grep plus file reads

The baseline is a literal search followed by reading the relevant files or line
ranges. That is often enough for a short task. dctx earns its place when exact
symbol reads and outlines avoid repeatedly sending large, irrelevant files.
It aims to be one context-management tool across these workflows; choose the
surface that fits in [Choosing how to use dctx](MODALITIES.md).

### A small worked example

Run with dctx 1.1.0 on a copy of this repository's `crates/dctx-lex-go` folder. The output is real and complete.

```text
$ dctx map find Add
# dctx-lex-go find
s:tests/fixtures/basic.go#Add	fn	L43-45

$ dctx map read 's:tests/fixtures/basic.go#Add'
# dctx-lex-go read
s:tests/fixtures/basic.go#Add	fn	tests/fixtures/basic.go
func Add[T ~int](a, b T) T {
	return a
}

$ dctx map neighbors 's:tests/fixtures/basic.go#Add' --edge calls --dir in
# dctx-lex-go neighbors
calls:in:s:tests/fixtures/basic.go#main	fn	tests/fixtures/basic.go	L59
```

`find` returns a stable id, the kind of thing it is (a function) and its lines. This is a historical 1.1.0 transcript; the current CLI also includes verified source bytes in text `read` output, or in `source_utf8` with `read --json`. `neighbors` says that `main` calls it, on line 59.

## The philosophy

The [specification](SPEC.md#2-the-core-belief-prompt-processing-efficiency) turns this into five testable rules.

**Bounded.** Every map answer has a size ceiling, reserved before anything is written, and a record is never split. The budget is up to 2,000 estimated tokens (1,000 for `explain`).
*Why it matters to you:* one question cannot flood the context window and crowd out your own instructions.

**Deterministic.** The same code and the same question give the same bytes.
*Why it matters to you:* results are repeatable, and repeated prompts can be served from a cache.

**Prefix-stable.** When context is sent again across turns, bytes that did not need to change do not change.
*Why it matters to you:* this is what keeps caching working across a conversation.

**Non-redundant.** Within one session, do not resend what was already sent unless it changed. This one is still a target.

**Honest.** Every answer states its freshness, precision and provenance, and dctx never asserts what it does not know. With `--json`, the `read` above carries `"freshness":{"mode":"strict","state":"verified"}`, a `precision` block, and `more` and `next` fields for anything that did not fit. Calls it cannot resolve are listed as `unresolved`, not guessed.
*Why it matters to you:* you and your assistant can tell a fact from a guess.

The docs add a few more commitments:

- **Offline.** No telemetry, no update checks, no model calls. A release check counted zero network connections across 16 commands. Nothing leaves your machine.
- **Private by default.** A file is classified before any byte of it is read. Secret-shaped files such as `.env`, `*.pem` and `id_rsa` are listed with content omitted, with no override in v1.
- **No embeddings.** dctx does not turn code into vectors and search by similarity. It ranks by names and syntax.
- **Features must earn their place.** A feature without a measured acceptance gate is not a dctx feature.

## Why byte-identical output matters

### Prompt caching, in plain words

Much of each request to an AI model repeats the last one: system instructions, project context, earlier turns. Providers keep a cache of prompt beginnings. If the **start** of a new prompt matches a cached one exactly, byte for byte, they reuse their earlier work on that part. Cached input costs a fraction of the normal price and is processed faster.

The match must be exact, and it is checked from the beginning. Picture a reader who remembers the first fifty pages you sent earlier. Send the same fifty pages and they skip ahead. Change one word on page two, and from that word on they must read everything again, even if pages three to fifty are unchanged.

So one changed byte early in a prompt (a timestamp, a file listed in a different order, a file size) breaks the cache for everything after it.

### Prefix-stable, simply

"Prefix" means the beginning of a text. "Prefix-stable" means the beginning stays the same unless the content there really changed. Edit one file, and only the bytes from that file onward should differ.

Timestamps are the classic problem. In 1.0.0, every line of the `dctx pack` file tree carried a modification time, and file lines a size. The tree sits near the top, so merely re-saving a file (a `touch`) changed almost the whole page as far as a cache is concerned. Since 1.1.0 tree lines carry only an id. A bare `touch` leaves the output byte-identical, and an edit keeps everything before the edited file as a shared prefix. `--tree-stamps=on` brings back the old lines.

In the same folder we appended one comment line to the last file in the tree, `tests/review_lexers_a.rs`, and compared `dctx pack .` before and after:

```text
default output:      first 117,215 of 122,437 bytes unchanged
--tree-stamps=on:    first   2,151 of 123,159 bytes unchanged
```

By default about 96% of the page is still a reusable prefix. With timestamps on, almost nothing is.

### The evidence

The [stability report](research/stability-20261105/REPORT.md) measured map answers on 6 November 2026, on three pinned local corpora with 11 kinds of question each. **33 of 33** text answers and **33 of 33** JSON answers were byte-identical after an unrelated edit elsewhere in the project, and all were identical over five separate runs.

The report states its limits too. It measures dctx's answers, not a provider's cache hits. It ran on Linux only. The layered design that would keep context prefix-stable across a whole conversation ([SPEC §12.1](SPEC.md#121-prefix-stable-tiers-target)) is still a target.

### An illustration of money and time

*Made-up numbers, not any provider's prices.* Assume:

- an agent sends the same 20,000 tokens of project context on each of 10 turns;
- normal input costs 10 units per 1,000 tokens, cached input 1 unit;
- the cache holds between turns.

If the context is byte-identical, turn one pays 200 units and the next nine pay 20 each: 380 units. If a timestamp near the top changes every turn, every turn pays 200: 2,000 units. The model also re-reads all 20,000 tokens every turn instead of reusing them, so each answer takes longer. Real ratios differ by provider; the mechanism is the same.

### Other reasons determinism matters

- **Reproducible reviews.** A colleague who runs the same command on the same code sees exactly what the assistant saw.
- **Meaningful diffs.** If saved context changes, the code changed, not a clock or a sort order.
- **Trust.** A tool whose answers shift for no reason is hard to rely on. In the spec's words, "trust is the product".

## What dctx is not

- **Not a type checker.** Call edges come from names, scopes and imports; ambiguous references are dropped.
- **Not exact token counting.** Budgets use an estimate, `ceil(2 × UTF-8 bytes / 7)`, not a model's tokenizer.
- **Not vector search or RAG.** No embeddings in the core, and the engine never calls a model.
- **Not a hosted service or a daemon.** One binary that runs when you call it. No telemetry, not even opt-out.
- **Limits still matter.** Plain `dctx pack` sends the selected project without an output budget by default. A 100 GB tree needs scoping, and the cache has a 2 GiB hard cap. CI covers Linux, macOS and Windows; byte-stability measurements here ran on Linux only.

# DTS source v2 and compiled plan IR v1

Status: current versioned design sketch; proposed syntax is not a release promise.
Defines organization control of every mode under the accepted structure.
Depends on API, identity and parser contracts; shared by the facade and mode engines.
Preserves the v1 compiler/rendering contract while extending typed policy.

## Compatibility and typed plan

DTS v1 variables, partials, layouts, four marker definitions, static resolution
and runtime data injection remain valid with byte-identical fixture outputs.
A version declaration selects v2; never infer version by an unknown field.
Legacy defaults compile to an explicit pack plan. Every map/future mode request
also receives a compiled default/custom plan; there is no second hidden policy
language or engine path bypassing DTS.

```text
ContextPlanV1 = {
  source_language_version, ir_major:1, ir_minor:0,
  required_capabilities, selection_rules, extraction_rules,
  budget_rules, views, render_program,
  selection_digest, extraction_digest, render_digest, plan_digest
}
```

| Typed section | Responsibility | Validation |
|---|---|---|
| SELECT | Paths/languages/kinds and Include/Exclude/OmitContent/DebugVisible policy | Root-relative paths, bounded rule count, no grant expansion |
| INDEX | Requested facts, parser/dialect, extraction limits | Available parser capability; Rust default `syn`; optional native only explicit |
| BUDGET | Final bytes/estimated tokens, records/depth, parse/memory/work bounds | Nonnegative bounded quantities; intersect host/mode ceilings; overflow refused |
| VIEW | Pack/map/future projection naming selection/extraction/budget/render refs | All references resolved, acyclic, mode capability present |
| RENDER | Existing partials/layout/markers plus bounded record iteration | No arbitrary evaluation, filesystem/network/process access or loaded plugins |

Source examples in proposal §2 are illustrative; B2 freezes precise grammar
and source fixtures before parser implementation. The typed semantics above
are normative. Custom source is built with explicit `template build`; shipped
compiled defaults need no runtime source parse. Template *sources* remain
user-owned; compiled plans are reconstructible cache entries.

## Permission and budgets

`permission = host_grant ∩ organization_ceiling ∩ session_selection`.
Within that ceiling, preserve existing ordered last-match ignore/omit semantics.
A template can narrow access but never turn a host denial into Include.
DebugVisible authorizes metadata only. Read rule/config sources through explicit
capabilities; unreadable policy is `PolicyUnavailable`, never default-allow.
Compiled plans bind their policy inputs/revision; changed/removed policy sources
invalidate authorization before cached facts or render output can be served.

Selection/extraction digests change index validity independently. Rendering-only
changes do not reparse source; they still change the plan/render digest and
continuation compatibility. A parser capability/revision change alters FactKey.
Budget/depth narrowing cannot make previously unauthorized facts visible.

Final-output token estimate is `ceil(2 * UTF8_bytes / 7)` over the complete
encoded answer. Rendering reserves headers, delimiters, escaping and continuation
before choosing whole records. Loops traverse only authorized records under
iteration/work bounds. Cyclic partials, unknown variables/opcodes, missing
capabilities and impossible envelopes are typed errors; no fallback rendering
that violates the configured mode or privacy ceiling.

## Compiled IR envelope

IR magic `DCTXIR\0\0` (8 bytes), major/minor u16, exact total length u64,
required capability bitset u64, section_count u32, followed by bounded typed
sections. Each section has `kind:u16, schema:u16, length:u32, payload[length]`.
Trailing SHA-256 covers all preceding bytes. Integer encoding is little-endian;
strings have checked u32 byte lengths and UTF-8. Maximum plan 1 MiB, 64 sections,
10,000 instructions; caller may narrow. Unknown required section/opcode/version
refuses load. No native-memory layout or executable serialized pointers.

Canonical sections order SELECT/INDEX/BUDGET/VIEW/RENDER/provenance, sorted named
definitions with source rule order preserved inside each. Domain-separated
identity framing (identity v1 kind 8) defines plan_digest; render_digest uses
kind 8 with a distinct IR schema/domain payload identifying render-only input.
Selection uses kind 4, extraction kind 5. B2 supplies canonical encoding goldens
and corruption fuzzing before compiled IR is a release format.

## Owner tests and model

B2 owns v1 parity, v2 compile/load determinism, section/opcode rejection and
positive controls; P1 authorization-before-render, P5 final budget, P6 frozen
clock/reordered-input equality. Model compile→validated-plan→authorized-view→
bounded-render transitions and policy-epoch revocation. Mutation removing the
host intersection must fail a denied-content test. Mutation budgeting unescaped
strings must fail a Unicode/JSON envelope property. Unsupported parser tests
include a positive `syn` capability case and explicit optional tree-sitter case.
Future modes must add their typed VIEW capability and conformance fixture to
this same compiler/facade contract before release.

# AGENTS.md snippet: task context from dctx

Paste the section below into a project's `AGENTS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md`) so coding agents start from dctx context.

## Notes for coding agents

Before editing, pull the code your task names, cut to a budget:

```sh
dctx pack --for "$TASK" --budget 3000
```

`$TASK` is the task description. dctx runs `map find` on the names the text mentions (backticked words, snake_case,
camelCase, `a::b`, then longer plain words), then `map neighbors` and `map read` on the best hits, and prints whole lines
until the budget is spent. The budget is in estimated tokens, ceil(2 × UTF-8 bytes / 7), not a tokenizer count. The last
line reports the estimate and how many lines were dropped. Exit 1 means no name in the text matched the index.

Name things in the text: `--for main` or `--for Session` works, but a sentence such as "how does caching work" only
matches loose words, and dctx says so on stderr (the page itself is unchanged). Put a short name next to prose in
backticks, as in ``--for 'fix `run` in the pack command'``.

Then narrow with `dctx map find`, `dctx map neighbors <id>` and `dctx map read <id>` as needed (`dctx map --help`).

# Map mode

Map mode explores a project through bounded outlines, symbol searches and source
reads. It builds the index automatically; there is no user `index` command.
The current CLI uses the shared dctx facade. Older storage and Git-based designs
in [SPEC-MAP-MODE](../SPEC-MAP-MODE.md) are not the current CLI contract.
dctx and this guide are Apache-2.0.

For a tool client, see the [MCP server guide](MCP.md), including the opt-in lean
profile and custom tool subsets.

## Commands

```text
dctx map <map|find|neighbors|explain|read|skeleton|grep> <TARGET> [OPTIONS]
dctx map hubs [--limit N] [--json] [--place PATH] [--budget TOKENS] [--meta]
dctx map path <FROM> <TO> [--json] [--place PATH] [--budget TOKENS] [--meta]
dctx map export [--format json|mermaid] [--output PATH] [--place PATH]
```

| Verb | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `map TARGET` | Outline a place-relative file or a node; TARGET is required (omitting it does not scan). |
| `find TARGET` | Search for a name or concept; quote multiword targets. |
| `neighbors TARGET` | Inspect a node's relations. |
| `explain TARGET` | Inspect one node's details. |
| `read TARGET` | Read a node's verified source; a long node pages with `--cursor`. `dctx read` is the same verb. |
| `skeleton FILE` | A file's (or `m:<path>`'s) declaration signatures in source order, no bodies. |
| `grep LITERAL` | Exhaustive literal search of indexed files, hits grouped by enclosing symbol. |
| `hubs` | Most-called symbols and per-directory file and symbol counts. No TARGET. |
| `path FROM TO` | Shortest edge path (calls, imports, contains; either direction; at most 8 hops), or `no path`. |
| `export` | The whole graph as one deterministic JSON or Mermaid document; no token cap. |

Copy node IDs from results: `m:sample.py` names a module and
`s:sample.py#PythonBeacon` names a symbol. `dctx map <verb> --help` prints each
verb's own page and example.

The following option descriptions follow `dctx map --help`
([source](../../crates/dctx-cli/src/map/args.rs)):

| Option | Meaning / bounds |
| --- | --- |
| `--json` | Facade JSON v2, including the precision label. |
| `--place PATH` | Place or worktree root; default: current directory. |
| `--meta` | Restore the snapshot digest and generation in the text header and JSON. Without it, answer bytes do not change across unrelated edits or time. |
| `--profile` | Stage timings and the five slowest files on stderr (`DCTX_PROFILE=1` is the same switch). |
| `--budget TOKENS` | Output tokens, 1..2000; `explain` max: 1000. `read` with no `--budget` uses the 2,000-token hard cap. |
| `--depth N` | `map`: 1..3; `neighbors`: 1..4. `explain` and `read` take no depth. |
| `--limit N` | `map`, `find`, `neighbors` page size; `explain` and `read` accept only 1. `hubs`: 1..60 lines, default 20. |
| `--offset N` | Refused. Pass the previous page's `next` value to `--cursor`. |
| `--cursor TOKEN` | Opaque continuation. A stale token is rejected. |
| `--kind fn,type,doc` | `find`: comma-separated node kinds. |
| `--in PATH` | `find` or `grep`: restrict to a relative path. |
| `-i`, `--ignore-case` | `grep`: ASCII case-insensitive match. |
| `--edge calls,imports` | `neighbors`: comma-separated edge filter. |
| `--dir in\|out\|both` | `neighbors`: relation direction. |
| `--lines A-B --full` | `read`: exactly those absolute source lines inside the node; `--full` permits 400. |
| `--rev SHA` | Refused: this build does not link Git. |

Environment bounds: `DCTX_MAX_SOURCE_BYTES` (total source bytes one scan may read,
default 1 GiB), `DCTX_MAX_RECORDS` (files, symbols and edges one index may hold,
default 1000000), `DCTX_MAX_ENTRIES` (files and directories one scan may visit,
default 100000) and `DCTX_FRESHNESS` (see below).

The parser also accepts these `--kind` values: `method`, `struct`, `enum`,
`trait`, `impl`, `const`, `macro`, `class`, `interface`, `symbol`, `module`,
`package`, `place`, `test`. Edge names also include `contains`, `implements`,
`uses-type`, `tests`, `documents`, `reexports`.

The token estimate is `ceil(2 * UTF-8 bytes / 7)`, not a tokenizer guarantee.

## Index, cache and privacy

Each invocation opens a facade session and can reuse a compatible persisted
map generation after checking its inventory and file freshness. The default
stamp mode trusts settled files with unchanged size, mtime and inode;
`DCTX_FRESHNESS=strict_live` hashes every file on a warm start. Exact source
reads still verify live bytes. There is no persistent CLI graph database.
The retired per-worktree SQLite cache selector (`map/storage.rs`) has been
deleted; the CLI does not read `DCTX_MAP_CACHE`.

The shared cache stores `ledger.v1`, `policy.v1`, serialized generations and
view manifests in managed object files. Generations contain file inventory,
digests and stamps, nodes, signatures, summaries, spans and edges, rather than
copies of all source contents. See [Choosing how to use dctx](../MODALITIES.md#huge-trees-scope-before-indexing)
for huge-tree scoping and the behavior when the cache cap is reached.
Set `DCTX_CACHE_DIR` to an
absolute path to override its root. Otherwise it is:

| Platform | Cache root |
| --- | --- |
| macOS | `~/Library/Caches/dctx/v2` |
| Windows | `%LOCALAPPDATA%/dctx/Cache/v2` |
| Other | `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/dctx/v2`, or `~/.cache/dctx/v2` |

The implemented lifecycle follows
[DX-ARCH-08](../archive/design/ARCHITECTURE-DECISIONS.md): time-based expiry, a system
size cap and an automatic cleaner. Defaults are 7 days for idle overlays/previews,
30 days for unpinned roots and 1 day for staging; the hard cap is 2 GiB, the soft
watermark 1.5 GiB and the eviction target 1.2 GiB. These are cache policies, not
a claim that every map query persists those object types.

```sh
dctx cache status --json
dctx cache gc --dry-run
dctx cache purge --root /absolute/project/path --dry-run
dctx cache purge --all --dry-run
dctx cache config auto off --max-bytes 1000000 --ttl-days 7
dctx cache auto
```

`status` accepts `--root PATH`; `gc` accepts `--root PATH`, `--max-bytes N` and
`--legacy`. Applying `purge` requires `--yes` and either `--root PATH` or `--all`.
`cache config` without arguments shows persisted policy; `auto on|off` controls
auto-clean, and `--max-bytes` can only tighten the cap. Pack, map, template,
plugin and TUI commands run one bounded cleanup when due (daily by default).
`--no-auto-clean` or `DCTX_AUTO_CLEAN=0` disables that slice.

Ignored files are excluded before content reads; omitted files may have metadata
listed but their content is never read. The host loads the global ignore file
(`<config dir>/dctx/ignore`: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/dctx/ignore` or
`~/.config/dctx/ignore` on Linux and macOS, `%APPDATA%\dctx\ignore` on Windows),
root and nested `.gitignore` rules, then the chosen root's `.dctxignore`.
`DCTX_INDEX_IGNORED=1` skips those ignore texts; built-in sensitive-file and
`.git` exclusions still apply. The core does not read Git metadata or run Git, so
`.git/info/exclude` and Git's `core.excludesFile` are not applied.
The optional Git plugin has separately disclosed authority; see [Plugins](PLUGINS.md).

# Plugins

A plugin adds commands or hooks through a bounded, versioned JSON protocol over
stdio. The host brokers its requested effects; installation, enablement,
capability consent and execution admission are separate steps. Bundled code can
run as a worker of the same executable; independently installed artifacts use
the plugin protocol. Availability is limited as described below.
dctx, the bundled Git plugin and this guide are Apache-2.0.

## Bundled Git plugin and consent

The default CLI includes `dctx/git` version `1.0.0`, with alias `dctx git` and
the verbs `status` and `protect`. The catalog defaults to enabled. A fresh CLI
without a consent record reports `enabled` with `needs-consent`; shipping the
worker does not grant its capabilities or guarantee that it can launch.
`dctx git` is a plugin alias, not a general Git passthrough.

The [bundled manifest capabilities](../../crates/dctx-cli/src/plugin/bundled.rs)
disclose these grants:

| Capability | Bound |
| --- | --- |
| Required `file.read` | Project `.gitignore`, at most 1,048,576 bytes. |
| Required `file.write` | Existing project `.gitignore` only (`create=false`); growth at most 4,096 bytes, total at most 1,052,672 bytes. |
| Optional `program.run` | Program `git`, operation `git.add-ignore`, resource `git-admin:stage-ignore`, output at most 65,536 bytes. |
| Outputs / network | Neither requested. |

This narrow optional Git recipe belongs to the plugin boundary. The map/core
does not run Git, read `.git/` or use Git hashes for identity.

Review the requested capabilities before approving:

```sh
dctx plugin list
dctx plugin info dctx/git --json
dctx plugin enable dctx/git --approve
dctx plugin disable dctx/git
```

`--approve` records consent for the displayed capability set. New installations
remain inactive until enabled; combined `install --enable` requires `--approve`.
Capability expansion can require fresh consent. Explicit disable persists
across updates. `enable --project PATH` scopes consent to a project; omitting it
uses user scope. `disable --project PATH` is accepted/reported, but the current
CLI disable operation is user-wide.

The desktop presents these states:

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `enabled` | Enabled in the registry; execution still requires admission. |
| `needs-consent` | Review and approve the requested capabilities. |
| `disabled` | Disabled by the user. |
| `failed` | A failure is reported; inspect the last failure message. |

The CLI additionally separates enablement (`inactive`, `enabled`, `disabled`)
from consent (`inactive`, `needs-consent`, `granted`, `disabled`) and reports
worker availability. A strict build lists the bundled catalog as disabled,
with consent `unavailable` and worker `excluded`.

## CLI reference

These are the command shapes from the plugin help renderer
([`render.rs`](../../crates/dctx-cli/src/plugin/render.rs)) and
[`parse.rs`](../../crates/dctx-cli/src/plugin/parse.rs):

```text
dctx plugin search [query] [--refresh] [--json]
dctx plugin install <owner/repo>[@version] [--enable --approve] [--json]
dctx plugin install --url <https-url> --id <publisher/name> [--json]
dctx plugin install --file <bundle> --id <publisher/name> [--json]
dctx plugin list [--json]
dctx plugin info <id> [--json]
dctx plugin enable <id> [--project <path>] [--approve] [--json]
dctx plugin disable <id> [--project <path>] [--json]
dctx plugin remove <id> [--json]
dctx plugin update [<id>] [--version <version>] [--check] [--json]
dctx plugin verify [<id>] [--refresh-trust] [--json]
dctx plugin run <id> -- <args>
dctx git <status|protect>
```

`dctx plugin`, `dctx plugin help`, `--help` and `-h` show plugin help.
Search accepts one query argument; quote phrases. Search and list use cached
metadata; `search --refresh` requests a fetch. List and help start no worker,
fetch nothing and do not create a project `.dctx/` directory.

Install accepts exactly one source: repository locator, HTTPS manifest URL or
offline bundle. URL/file sources require `--id`; the parser also accepts
`--enable --approve` with those sources. `update --check` reports a candidate
without downloading; omitting the ID in update/verify selects the bundled plugin.
`verify --refresh-trust` requests a revocation freshness check. Bundled updates
come with the containing CLI/app release. `remove` masks the bundled copy when
applicable. The current product's offline limits still apply to these commands.

`run` requires the `--` separator. The Git alias rejects that separator.
The parser recognizes `--json` for plugin and alias requests, including `run`,
and strips it before forwarding plugin arguments.

## Desktop: Settings > Plugins

Open **Settings > Plugins** to inspect bundled/installed source, version,
state, requested capabilities and the last failure. **Refresh plugins** reloads
the list. **Enable** and **Disable** call the host management API.
**Grant consent** opens a review dialog with plugin ID, version, artifact
SHA-256, capability descriptions and exact grants/bounds. **Confirm grant**
records user-wide consent for all projects; **Cancel** closes the dialog.
**Check for update** reports cached information and explicitly states that
online discovery is unavailable. These behaviors are implemented in
[`plugins.ts`](../../apps/dctx-desktop/src/plugins.ts); opening settings does
not itself execute plugin code or fetch from a network.

## Strict build

The [`dctx` library](../../crates/dctx/Cargo.toml) includes the optional
`plugin-runtime` feature in its defaults. Hosts requiring the engine without
that runtime must disable defaults and select `pack`, `map`, `templates`, `fs`,
`segments`, `cache` as needed. The runtime adds the host, platform and protocol
dependencies; sessions still require an explicit host.

For the [CLI](../../crates/dctx-cli/Cargo.toml), select
`--no-default-features --features strict` when building. Cargo features are
additive: selecting `strict` alone leaves defaults enabled. This composition
excludes `dctx-plugin-host`, `dctx-plugin-platform` and `dctx-plugin-git` from
normal dependencies. Management metadata/protocol/distribution code remains;
strict does not mean that every crate whose name contains `plugin` disappears.

## Trust and signatures

Distribution verifies detached Ed25519 signatures over domain-separated exact
manifest/index bytes, checks SHA-256 artifact integrity, and uses pinned
publisher keys, revocation freshness and rollback checks. A key downloaded
beside an artifact is not an independent trust anchor. Verification does not
grant capabilities or establish confinement. The production verifier never
signs or generates keys; signing belongs only in separate release tooling
(test fixtures use test keys). **Unverified:** a completed production release
signing tool in this checkout; the design describes it as separate work.
The product CLI currently supplies no index key and no TLS network adapter.

## What is not yet available

- Qualified native plugin launch on any OS. Linux has restricted-process
  building blocks, but arbitrary third-party ELF launch remains unsupported;
  macOS lacks the reviewed Seatbelt/initial-exec composition; Windows and other
  targets are unsupported. The platform provider also refuses bundled launch
  and the Git recipe. A consent record cannot bypass these admission failures.
- Online discovery, downloads and updates in the current product wiring.
  Search can inspect cached metadata and the distribution engine supports
  verified offline bundles, but network refresh needs a configured trust key
  and network adapter. The desktop explicitly reports offline update discovery.
- Public plugin publication through this CLI. There is no `plugin publish`
  command. The default discovery URL is `https://example.invalid/dctx/index.json`;
  a live public registry/release publication is **unverified**. Local index
  tooling and signed fixture tests do not establish public availability.

Sources: [plugin design](../design/PLUGINS.md),
[native platform limits](../../crates/dctx-plugin-platform/README.md),
[Ed25519 verification](../../crates/dctx-plugin-distribution/src/domain/signature.rs),
and the [crate map](../CRATE-MAP.md).

Default budgets and default output are used, without `--meta` in the measured

## M7 and acceptance limits

For each transition, M7 = longest common **byte** prefix of previous and current

The same-request trace is each case's five warm answers followed by its post-edit

transitions per stream, 390 total. Text and JSON are separate context-block streams.
These are recorded tool-answer traces, with one answer treated as one injected

The local unrelated-edit and five-run JSON gates pass. The low changing-question

The three text `read` pages actually include their selected source bodies. Text

# dctx vs Trail-Code: head-to-head benchmark (October 2026)

Isolated, reproducible comparison of two code-context tools for coding agents on seven real corpora
and one synthetic adversarial corpus. Every number below comes from `data/raw/*.jsonl` and can be
regenerated with `scripts/`. Where Trail-Code is better, this report says so plainly.

- **dctx** at commit `17dff0b454c24f43848abad1c88ea982e02731f7` (branch `internal`), `dctx-cli v0.25.0`,
  agent interface `dctx map <map|find|neighbors|explain|read>`.
- **Trail-Code** `@trailhq/trail-code@0.23.1` from npm (repository HEAD `b1211efd`, whose
  `package.json` is also 0.23.1), CLI `trail` plus its MCP server.

## 1. Summary

| Area | Result |
|---|---|
| Call graph (callers, depth 1) | **Trail-Code wins decisively.** Trail precision 0.94 to 1.00, recall 0.10 to 0.96 per corpus. dctx returns **no call or import edges at all** (recall 0 on 140 targets): the CLI facade only emits `contains` edges. |
| Task-level answers (70 agent questions) | Trail 122/140 points, 312/354 gold facts in 88.7k tokens. dctx 69/140, 169/354 in 500k tokens (480k of them from the unbounded legacy tree used as the only overview). Without the overview question dctx uses 19.2k tokens for 137/322 facts (7.15 facts/1k tokens) versus Trail 57.0k for 284/322 (4.98 facts/1k): dctx is terser, Trail answers about twice as much. |
| Footprint | **dctx wins.** One 9.2 MB binary (libc, libm, libgcc_s) versus 405.6 MB of `node_modules` (8,567 files, 50 package versions) plus a Node runtime. |
| Cold index | **dctx wins** on all seven corpora: 0.09 to 6.05 s versus 2.44 to 94.9 s (2.8 to 69 times faster); peak RSS 8 to 567 MiB versus 181 to 2,111 MiB. Trail's index is smaller only on core (65 MB versus 158 MB). |
| Warm query latency | **dctx wins** on small and medium repos (30 to 260 ms versus 0.6 to 1.4 s; Node startup sets Trail's floor near 0.6 s). On the largest Rust corpus dctx re-reads a 158 MB generation per process (1.45 s, 370 MiB per query) and Trail's `callers` is faster (0.83 s). |
| Freshness | **Tie on correctness**: both see unstaged, untracked and staged edits and drop reverted symbols. Trail also adds the caller edge to the new function; dctx cannot. dctx's first query after an edit costs a full re-index (core: 7.5 s), and every edit adds a full new generation to the cache (core: 158 MB to 946 MB). |
| Cache-friendliness | **Trail wins.** Trail text outputs are byte-identical across runs and across unrelated edits. Every dctx answer starts with a header containing the snapshot digest, so any edit anywhere changes byte 21 to 50 of every answer; dctx JSON is never byte-identical twice (`age_s`). |
| Bounding | **dctx wins for map verbs** (hard 2,000-token cap, never exceeded; budgets below the minimum record size are refused with exit 1). Trail has no budget flag; single answers reached 142 KB (40.6k tokens). dctx's legacy tree and `pack` are unbounded (974 KB tree on django; 8.7 MB pack). |
| Privacy / network | **dctx wins.** Zero sockets in every audited dctx run and no writes to the repository in map mode. Trail does a daily npm version check that ignores `DO_NOT_TRACK`, records an install telemetry event in `postinstall` and tries to send it, and modifies `.gitignore` and adds `.ignore` on every `trail build`. dctx `pack` printed a fake `.env` secret; Trail never read `.env`. |
| Language breadth | Trail parses 23 languages, including Scala, Elixir, Lua, OCaml, Zig, Dart, Solidity and Vue; dctx parses none of those. dctx adds structure for Markdown, JSON, TOML and YAML, which Trail ignores. |

## 2. Methodology

### Host, isolation, contention

- VM `build-host`: 32 vCPU Intel Xeon E5-2680 v2 @ 2.80 GHz, 94 GB RAM, Debian 13, kernel
  6.12.111, Node v24.22.0, npm 11.19.1, rustc/cargo 1.99.0 (`data/env.txt`).
- The VM was also running an unrelated build and mutation batch. Every benchmark command was pinned with
  `taskset -c 24-31` (8 CPUs). The other batch was not pinned, so it could share those CPUs.
  1-minute load average across the 3,398 measured runs: min 1.04, median 2.31, p95 8.46, max 16.03
  (each row in `data/raw/*runs.jsonl` records load before and after; `phases.jsonl` records each phase).
  The ripgrep and pocketbase query phases ran at load 8 to 10, so treat their Trail `find` times
  (1.2 to 1.3 s) as contention-affected.
- Both tools ran as the dedicated unprivileged user `dctxbench`, with `HOME`, npm prefix, npm cache,
  `XDG_CACHE_HOME` and `DCTX_CACHE_DIR` inside `/path/to/workdir/dctx-vs-trail`, through `scripts/benv`
  (`env -i`, then `sudo -u dctxbench unshare -rn`, then `taskset`). After installs, clones and builds,
  every measured command ran in a new network namespace with only a down loopback.
- `DO_NOT_TRACK=1` (Trail's documented opt-out, `dist/telemetry/gate.js`) was set for every measured
  Trail run except the two deliberate "telemetry on" network audits.
- Timing: GNU time 1.9 (`/usr/bin/time -v`, 10 ms resolution) records wall, user+sys CPU and peak RSS for
  the tool process tree. Warm queries are medians of 5 runs, cold runs medians of 3.
- Output size: raw stdout bytes and `ceil(bytes / 3.5)` estimated tokens for both tools (identical to
  dctx's own `ceil(2*bytes/7)`). This is an estimate, not a tokenizer.
- Page cache was not dropped, to avoid disturbing the co-tenant batch. "Cold" therefore means "no tool
  index or cache", not "cold disk".

### Builds and versions

- dctx: source rsynced from the workstation (no `target/`), built with `cargo build --release --locked
  -p dctx-cli -j 8` without a compiler cache: 98.7 s wall, 389 s user CPU. Binary: 9,207,072 bytes,
  sha256 `26c3cb70...cbce`. `ldd`: `libgcc_s`, `libm`, `libc`, `ld-linux` only.
- Trail-Code: `npm install --save-exact @trailhq/trail-code@0.23.1` (39.96 s). npm 11.19 printed
  "install scripts not yet covered by allowScripts" warnings but still ran them (13 packages, including
  Trail's own `postinstall` and `node-gyp` builds; Node headers were downloaded into `~/.cache/node-gyp`).

### Corpora (pinned)

| Corpus | Language | Pin | Tracked files |
|---|---|---|---|
| flask | Python | tag 3.1.3, `22d92470` | 235 |
| ripgrep | Rust | tag 15.2.0, `e89fff89` | 222 |
| pocketbase | Go + JS | tag v0.40.5, `6f370ea7` | 924 |
| trailcode (Trail-Code repo) | TypeScript | `b1211efd` | 380 |
| dctx | Rust (+ fixtures in 15 languages) | `17dff0b4` | 1,749 |
| django | Python | tag 6.1.2, `2212534b` | 7,071 |
| core (private Rust repository) | Rust | `f5f2f48b` | 3,190 |
| adversarial (generated) | mixed | `scripts/gen_adversarial.py` | see section 10 |

`core` was copied without `target/` and `corpus/`; its `.agent/worktrees/` (copies of the tree) was also
removed. Its raw outputs, symbol names, paths and source lines are **redacted** from `data/`
(`scripts/redact_private.py`); only numbers are published.

### Gold sets and scoring

- **Targets.** `scripts/select_targets.py` picks 20 definitions per corpus with a fixed seed: 4 hubs
  (unique name, many calls), 4 rare (1 to 3 calls), 4 receiver-called methods, 4 colliding names
  (2 to 6 definitions), 4 interface/trait methods. Selection uses the independent oracle in
  `scripts/goldlib.py`, not either tool.
- **Oracle.** Comments and strings are blanked (a cross-line state machine for Rust and Go, per-line for
  JS/TS, triple-quote aware for Python). A line is a call site of `N` only if `N` is directly followed by an
  argument list and the line is not a definition. Each site is bound to a definition by scope rules (same
  file or package, explicit import, `self`/`this`, `Type::`); receiver calls to names that also exist on
  standard-library types, and anything else unresolvable, are **ambiguous** and excluded from both
  precision and recall. Interface/trait targets are scored at name level: every site bound to some
  in-repo definition of the name, plus `self` calls.
- **Adjudication.** A Trail `calls` hit is a true positive if its span contains a gold site of the target,
  unjudged if it only contains ambiguous sites, and a false positive otherwise. Recall counts gold sites
  inside any reported hit. Collisions were spot-checked by hand (all 28 collision targets: sample sites
  listed in `data/targets/*.targets.json`). The hand check found one oracle bug: a `/*` inside a Rust
  multi-line doc string started a fake block comment. After the fix the gold was rebuilt for the **same**
  targets (`scripts/regold.py`; one target changed, ripgrep `unwrap_switch`, 61 to 69 sites), and the ripgrep
  accuracy and task phases were rerun. The earlier rows are kept in `data/raw/*.pre-regold`. A remaining
  known oracle gap: calls inside Python f-strings and JS template literals are blanked, which made
  one true Trail hit (flask `dumps`) count as a false positive.
- **Tasks.** `scripts/phase_tasks.py` builds 10 questions per corpus from the same oracle with fixed
  command sequences per tool. Facts are scored by presence in the outputs (JSON string values are also
  searched); caller facts must come from a caller/impact answer and need the caller's path and one of its
  call-line numbers. Score per question: 2 if at least 80% of facts are present, 1 if any, 0 otherwise.

## 3. Footprint

| | dctx | Trail-Code |
|---|---|---|
| Install | one binary, 9,207,072 bytes | `node_modules` 405,601,700 bytes, 8,567 files |
| Dependencies | 46 external crates in `cargo tree -e normal` (see TC-F11) | 50 package versions (47 names) in `npm ls --all`; largest: `tree-sitter-wasm` 128 MB, `@trailhq/trail-code` 129 MB (bundled grammars), `tree-sitter-swift` 73 MB, two LLM-provider SDKs 34 MB and 14 MB (used only by `--deep`) |
| Runtime | libc, libm, libgcc_s | Node >= 20 plus native addons |
| Install side effects | none | `postinstall` records an anonymous install event and spawns a detached flush; `~/.graft/telemetry.json` and `~/.graft/update-check.json` created at install |
| MCP | none (listed as planned in README) | 6 tools; tool definitions 3,515 bytes (~1,005 tokens) per agent session |

## 4. Indexing (section 2 of the brief)

Cold = new copy, no tool state, median of 3. dctx has no index command, so its cold run is the first
`dctx map find main` with an empty `DCTX_CACHE_DIR`. The Trail cold run is `trail build .`. No-op = repeat
with nothing changed (dctx: same query; Trail: `trail build .` again and `trail build --check .`).

| Corpus | dctx cold s (CPU s) | Trail cold s (CPU s) | dctx peak RSS MiB | Trail peak RSS MiB | dctx cache MB | Trail index MB | dctx no-op s | Trail no-op build s | Trail `--check` s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| flask | **0.09** (0.08) | 3.45 (3.88) | **8** | 181 | **0.85** | 4.39 | **0.04** | 0.88 | 3.29 |
| ripgrep | **0.45** (0.42) | 2.44 (3.40) | **18** | 282 | **1.77** | 8.36 | **0.05** | 1.35 | 1.97 |
| pocketbase | **0.72** (0.71) | 49.45 (51.42) | **39** | 969 | **6.69** | 41.83 | **0.17** | 2.65 | 49.52 |
| trailcode | **0.31** (0.30) | 17.83 (18.65) | **17** | 452 | **3.56** | 13.70 | **0.08** | 1.58 | 18.67 |
| dctx | **2.42** (2.38) | 9.74 (13.96) | **64** | 834 | **14.88** | 42.68 | **0.27** | 3.81 | 7.90 |
| django | **2.48** (2.46) | 94.89 (97.55) | **92** | 2,111 | **23.30** | 167.48 | **0.81** | 9.15 | 86.46 |
| core | **6.05** (7.02) | 16.88 (21.43) | **567** | 916 | 157.70 | **64.71** | **1.34** | 4.66 | 13.82 |

  nothing into the repository and nothing into `HOME` (verified by full manifests before and after).

## 5. Query latency and output size (section 3 and 4)

Warm medians of 5 (wall seconds; bytes of the answer). Command mapping:

(the map verbs have no root overview, TC-F05) / `trail map`; grep = none / `trail grep 'N\('`.

| Corpus | find dctx | find Trail | callers dctx | callers Trail | outline dctx | outline Trail | read dctx | read Trail | overview dctx | overview Trail | grep Trail |
